paras: The manhunt for the assailant of Jane Cunningham was a search in March and April 1881 for an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a young white woman near Orangeburg, South Carolina, and escaping into a swamp. A News and Courier dispatch printed under the headline "A Negro Wants Lynching" said he was being "hotly pursued" and "may have a short shift" if found. Two Black men were arrested as suspects elsewhere; the Newberry Herald wrote that the first, reportedly forced to confess by threats with "the pistol and the rope," would probably have been lynched at Orangeburg.

According to a dispatch dated Orangeburg, March 14, the daughter of a white man named Cunningham was walking with her little sister to a neighbor's house, about four miles from town, when a Black man who had followed her attacked her. The governor later named her as Miss Jane Cunningham; a Vermont version gave her age as about 22.

When she resisted, he struck her senseless with a lightwood knot and dragged her to a swamp while her sister ran for help. Hearing people approach, he escaped into the swamp. She was reported dangerously ill, with one eye almost beaten out.

On Monday, March 28, a Black man was arrested in Newberry County, and a telegram from Newberry told the Orangeburg sheriff that he had confessed. In jail he gave a Herald reporter the name George Bouner, contradicted himself about having been in Orangeburg County, and described an assault much like the published one. The Herald called him "almost an idiot" and recalled an earlier false confession in Laurens County. The Orangeburg sheriff came to Newberry, doubted the identification and declined to take him, then sent a description of the assailant that did not fit the prisoner.

On April 22 Governor Johnson Hagood offered a fifty-dollar reward for the unknown "colored person" who had assaulted Cunningham, said to have used the names Govan Brown and William Johnson. By then a second suspect, John Joseph Jones, alias Joe Jones, had been arrested at his house in lower Richland County on a trial justice's warrant after a neighbor reported him. Jailed in Columbia, Jones said he could prove an alibi, and Cunningham's father went to bring his daughter or other witnesses to identify him.

Two physicians pronounced the Newberry prisoner a lunatic, and he was sent to the Asylum. No report of whether Jones was identified or released was found. No capture or trial of the man the governor described is reported.

The News and Courier's dispatch ran under the headline "A Negro Wants Lynching" in the Abbeville Press and Banner on March 16 and the Newberry Herald on March 23, and without a headline in the Pickens Sentinel on March 24. The headline and the closing remark that the fugitive "may have a short shift" anticipated a lynching without disapproval. A separate account in the Spirit of the Age of Woodstock, Vermont, on March 23 called the attacker "the fiend" and her recovery "extremely doubtful."

The Newberry Herald on March 30 called the prisoner "the wretch," but on April 6 judged his confession "not worth a copper" and called the reported threats, if true, "a grave offense and an outrage of law and order." The paper added that he would "very probably" have been lynched on such a confession had he been taken to Orangeburg. The Weekly Union Times printed the Orangeburg report of his confession under "In the Grasp of the Law" as late as April 8.

The Savannah Morning News reported Jones's arrest among its South Carolina notes, saying the assailant had probably "been caged at last" and calling him "the Orangeburg brute." The Orangeburg Times printed the governor's proclamation on April 28 and again on May 5.

The accounts differ on the date: the March 14 dispatch placed the attack on the preceding Friday, the Vermont version on a Thursday, and the governor's proclamation and the Newberry Herald on March 10. They also differ on the assailant's appearance: the governor described a stout, brown-skinned man of about eighteen and the sheriff a heavy man "almost a mulatto," while the Newberry prisoner was slight, nearly black and about 21.

reader.title: Manhunt for the assailant of Jane Cunningham
bases: A manhunt in which the fugitive was publicly threatened with lynching and a suspect was reportedly forced to confess by threats with pistol and rope; no one was reported killed or hurt (A1, A6).

The News and Courier dispatch, a separate wire version and the governor's proclamation agree on the assault and the assailant's flight (A1, A3, A9); the Newberry arrest is reported by two papers (A5, A7).

accounts.label: News and Courier dispatch
accounts.gist: A Black man assaulted Cunningham's daughter, dragged her to a swamp, fled when people approached, and was being hotly pursued; he 'may have a short shift' if found.

accounts.label: Vermont wire version
accounts.gist: The attack came Thursday on a lonely stretch of highway; the victim, about 22, was not expected to recover.

accounts.label: Newberry Herald
accounts.gist: First thought the Newberry prisoner the right man; a week later called him the wrong man and his confession, reportedly forced by threats with pistol and rope, worthless.

accounts.label: Governor's proclamation
accounts.gist: The assailant was unknown and had fled; $50 reward offered with a description and aliases.

framing.detail: The dispatch ran as 'A Negro Wants Lynching' and predicted a 'short shift' for the fugitive.
The Newberry Herald called the suspect 'the wretch', then condemned the forced confession as 'an outrage of law and order' and noted he would probably have been lynched.
Savannah Morning News reported Jones 'caged at last', calling the assailant 'the Orangeburg brute'.

conflicts.note: The governor's proclamation is the formal statement and gives March 10; the dispatch says Friday.

Pursuit, plus threats with pistol and rope to force a confession from a suspect
Fugitive at large; two suspects later in custody (Newberry and Columbia jails)
